tasks.title: Revenue by month
tasks.statement: Output revenue (the sum of amount) by month: columns month (format YYYY-MM) and total, ordered by month.
tasks.hint: substr(day, 1, 7) gives "YYYY-MM"; GROUP BY this expression.

tasks.title: Joining the star
tasks.statement: Output revenue for each combination of product category and client city: columns category, city, total; ordered by category, then by city.
tasks.hint: Two INNER JOINs: to dim_product and to dim_client; group by two dimension columns.

tasks.title: Category share
tasks.statement: For each category output its share of total revenue in percent, rounded to an integer: columns category, pct; by share descending, ties by name.
tasks.hint: Take the grand total with a scalar subquery, multiply by 100.0.

tasks.title: Running revenue
tasks.statement: Output, by day, the revenue for the day and the running total: columns day, daily, running; ordered by day. Use a window function.
tasks.hint: First roll the facts up to days (a subquery), then SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY day).

tasks.title: Difference from the previous day
tasks.statement: For each day that has a previous day with sales, output the change in revenue: columns day, delta (the day's revenue minus the previous day's revenue); ordered by day.
tasks.hint: LAG(daily) OVER (ORDER BY day) gives the previous value; for the first day it is NULL, so remove that row.

tasks.title: Best product in a category
tasks.statement: For each category output the product with the highest revenue: columns category, name, total; ordered by category.
tasks.hint: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) on top of a grouping by product.

tasks.title: Totals like ROLLUP
tasks.statement: SQLite has no ROLLUP. Output revenue by category and the grand total in a single query: columns category, total; the last row has category = `TOTAL`. Order: categories alphabetically, the total last.
tasks.hint: UNION ALL of the grouping and the grand total; add a helper column for ordering.
tasks.starter:
-- totals by category and overall
SELECT

tasks.title: Cohorts by month of first purchase
tasks.statement: For each month of first purchase (cohort, format YYYY-MM) output the number of clients (clients) and how many of them also bought in the next calendar month (returned). Columns cohort, clients, returned; ordered by cohort. Months in the data are consecutive (Jan, Feb, Mar).
tasks.hint: First the month of each client's first purchase, then EXISTS: does the client have a purchase in the month "cohort + 1 month" (strftime(..., '+1 month')).

tasks.title: Funnel
tasks.statement: The table events(user_id, step, ts): steps 'view', 'cart', 'pay'. Output the funnel: the number of distinct users at each step, columns step, users; in the order view, cart, pay.
tasks.hint: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) by step; the order is set by a CASE in ORDER BY.

tasks.title: Dimension version on a date
tasks.statement: For each order output the client's city on the day of the order (the version where valid_from <= day < valid_to, and valid_to = NULL means "current"): columns id, city; ordered by id.
tasks.hint: The period condition goes in ON: valid_from <= day and (valid_to IS NULL OR day < valid_to).
tasks.starter:
-- city on the order date
SELECT

tasks.title: Close a version and add a new one
tasks.statement: Client 7 moved to Moscow on 2026-04-01. Close the current version (valid_to = '2026-04-01') and add a new one with city = `Moscow`, valid_from = '2026-04-01', valid_to = NULL. Do not touch client 8. The result is checked on the table.
tasks.hint: First UPDATE only the open version of client 7 (valid_to IS NULL), then INSERT.

tasks.title: Materialized table
tasks.statement: Create the table mv_daily(day, total), revenue by day, with CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT. The result is checked on its contents.
tasks.hint: CREATE TABLE mv_daily AS SELECT day, SUM(amount) AS total … GROUP BY day.
tasks.starter:

tasks.title: Topping up a pre-aggregate
tasks.statement: The table mv holds sums by day, but day d2 has grown (its sum in fact is 10), and day d3 has not arrived yet. With a single INSERT … ON CONFLICT refresh mv entirely from fact (insert new days, update total for existing ones). The result is checked on mv.
tasks.hint: INSERT … SELECT … GROUP BY day … ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE SET total = excluded.total; WHERE true is needed so ON CONFLICT parses.
tasks.starter:
-- recompute the pre-aggregate
INSERT INTO mv

tasks.title: Duplicates in a load
tasks.statement: In stage, events by id arrive many times with different version. Output one latest (highest version) record per id: columns id, version, payload; ordered by id.
tasks.hint: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY version DESC) and filter rn = 1.

tasks.title: Idempotent load
tasks.statement: Load stage into sales so that the run can be repeated: insert new ids, and for existing ones update day and amount. The result is checked on sales.
tasks.hint: ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET … = excluded.…
tasks.starter:
-- upsert from stage
INSERT INTO sales

tasks.title: Data quality checks
tasks.statement: Bad rows got into fact_sales. Output the ids of rows where there is no product in dim_product OR qty <= 0 OR amount < 0. Column id, ascending.
tasks.hint: LEFT JOIN to dim_product and check p.id IS NULL; plus conditions on qty and amount.

tasks.title: Best clients by city
tasks.statement: For each city output the client with the highest revenue: columns city, name, total; ordered by city.
tasks.hint: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) on top of a grouping by client.
tasks.starter:
-- best client in a city
SELECT

tasks.title: ROLLUP by hand
tasks.statement: Rows are lists [region, city, amount]. Write rollup_rows(rows): a list of rows [region, city, amount] in this order: for each region (alphabetically) its cities (alphabetically), then a subtotal [region, None, region's sum]; at the end the grand total [None, None, sum of all]. Empty input gives [[None, None, 0]].
tasks.hint: First a dictionary "region → city → amount", then walk it in sorted order.

tasks.title: Run-length compression
tasks.statement: A column of values is stored with run-length encoding. Write rle_encode(values): a list of pairs [value, run length] of consecutive equal values; an empty list gives an empty list.
tasks.hint: Watch the last pair: same value means increase the length, otherwise start a new pair.

tasks.title: From rows to columns
tasks.statement: A table is a list of row dictionaries, columns is the column order. Write rows_to_cols(rows, columns): a dictionary "column → list of values in row order" (a missing value is None). For an empty list of rows, empty lists.
tasks.hint: For each column, a list of r.get(c) values over the rows.

tasks.title: How much we read
tasks.statement: A table has rows rows and width bytes per row in total; a query reads columns of total size need bytes per row. Write scan_cost(rows, width, need): a pair [bytes for row storage, bytes for columnar storage] (in columnar storage without compression only the needed columns are read).
tasks.hint: Row storage reads the whole row, columnar storage reads only the needed columns.

tasks.title: Cleaning before a load
tasks.statement: Rows are lists [id, name, amount-as-string]. Write clean_rows(rows): keep rows whose amount is an integer (a minus sign is not allowed); the name is stripped of surrounding spaces and lowercased, the amount becomes int; for repeated ids keep only the first row. The result is a list of [id, name, amount] in the original order.
tasks.hint: Check with str.isdigit(); a set of ids already seen.

tasks.title: Load by partition replacement
tasks.statement: The warehouse is a dictionary "day → list of amounts". A new batch is a list of pairs [day, amount]. Loading by partition replacement: for each day present in the batch, the old data of that day is deleted and replaced by the batch's amounts (in batch order). Write load_partitions(store, batch): a new dictionary; do not modify the original. Repeating the same batch gives the same result.
tasks.hint: Build the new partitions from the batch and update a copy of the warehouse with them.

tasks.title: Applying a change stream
tasks.statement: Events are lists [number, operation, key, value], the operation is 'put' or 'del'. Apply them in ascending number order (even if they arrived out of order); an event with an already seen number is skipped (redelivery). Write apply_changes(events): the resulting dictionary "key → value".
tasks.hint: Sort by number, keep a set of seen numbers; put writes, del removes the key.

tasks.title: Dimension versions
tasks.statement: A client's history is a list of versions [city, from, to] (to = None for the current one), the changes are a list [date, city] in ascending date order. Write scd2_apply(history, changes): the new history. For each change with a city different from the current version's, the current one is closed with this date and a new [city, date, None] is added; a change with the same city is ignored. Do not modify the original list. Dates are strings YYYY-MM-DD.
tasks.hint: Copy the history; close "to" of the current version, then add a new one; skip an identical city.

tasks.title: Conversion funnel
tasks.statement: Events are lists [user, step]. steps is the order of funnel steps. A user counts at step k only if they passed all steps up to and including k (in any order of events). Write funnel(events, steps): the list of user counts at each step.
tasks.hint: A set of steps for each user; at step k it must contain steps[:k+1].

tasks.title: Cohort retention
tasks.statement: Purchases are lists [client, month], the month is an integer 1, 2, 3… A client's cohort is their first month. Write cohort_retention(purchases): a dictionary "cohort (as a string) → list [clients in the cohort, of them those who also bought in the next month]".
tasks.hint: A set of months for each client; the cohort is the minimum; retention means minimum + 1 is present.

tasks.title: Where to put the load
tasks.statement: Write pick_store(qps, rows_per_query, point_lookup): 'OLTP' if there are many queries (qps >= 100) and they are pinpoint (point_lookup is True) and read at most 100 rows; 'OLAP' if there are few queries (qps < 100) and each reads at least 100000 rows; otherwise 'reduce' (rethink the load).
tasks.hint: Two conditions and a default branch.
